KotlinCodingRules.keywords: kotlin, android, executable_specification, design_by_contract, kdoc, ai_to_ai, structural_anchors, null_safety, coroutines_structured_concurrency, sealed_exhaustiveness, immutability_default, scope_function_intent, yagni
KotlinCodingRules.Mission:
Canonical rules for writing Kotlin (Android baseline; Kotlin/JVM subset) for every execution-agent in the project.
Goal: turn each created or modified `.kt` / `.kts` (source) file into an «Executable Specification» — a readable, machine-parsable artifact in which intent, contract, and refactor hazards can be recovered from the file alone, without chat history or external documentation.
Baseline Kotlin rules layer; referenced from task tickets generated by `task-scaffolding`. Domain-specific conventions (DI frameworks, Jetpack Compose, KMP `expect/actual`) are NOT covered here; they live as separate directives layered on top. Logging discipline is a project-level concern and is NOT covered here.
Sources (public standards, cited by name; language cadence adapted for this ecosystem): official Kotlin coding conventions (kotlinlang.org/docs/coding-conventions.html) — naming, formatting discipline, immutability preference, scope-function intent, class-body order; official Android Kotlin style guide (developer.android.com/kotlin/style-guide) — visibility discipline, null-safety, Android-specific lifecycle safety notes; JetBrains Kotlin/Coroutines guides (kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-guide.html) — structured concurrency, dispatcher discipline, cancellation cooperation. Adopted as timeless engineering practice — version numbers, plugin lists, CLI flags, config snippets are intentionally omitted.
**Base axiom:** code will be read, parsed, and modified ONLY by other AI agents and AI IDEs (AI-to-AI ecosystem). Highest values: absolute predictability, semantic density, code introspectability. Comments are agent-authored machine comments — they expose intent, constraints, refactor hazards that code and types do not encode by themselves. English is for code and intent: all identifiers, KDoc, and intent comments strictly in English.

BeliefState.Axiom:
Non-null default. Nullable types (`T?`) declared only when the domain admits absence. The not-null assertion `!!` is forbidden except when the surrounding block carries an explicit `@invariant` naming the runtime guarantee that makes the assertion safe (e.g. «init-before-use ordering guaranteed by owning lifecycle»). Prefer safe call (`?.`), Elvis (`?:`), and smart-cast pattern (assign nullable to local `val` → smart-cast). Platform types from Java interop are wrapped at the boundary — never leaked into domain code.
Bare `!!` is a runtime landmine that names no invariant; a reader-agent cannot recover the intended guarantee from `!!` alone.

`val` is the default; `var` requires a justifying `@invariant` explaining the mutation lifecycle. Public surfaces expose `List` / `Set` / `Map` — never `MutableList` / `MutableSet` / `MutableMap`. Internal builders may hold mutable collections; expose immutable views (`.toList()` / `.toMap()`) at the API boundary. Data-class properties are `val`.
Mutability without an invariant is invisible policy: any reader-agent assumes «the value can change at any time» and cannot reason about the state machine.

Kotlin visibility modifiers are real at runtime — use them precisely. Default posture: - `private` for state and helpers confined to the declaring class / file. - `internal` for module-boundary contracts. - `public` only for surfaces named as external contracts. - `protected` for open-class inheritance edges only.
Omit `public` when it is the language default (per official Kotlin coding conventions). Never expand visibility to satisfy a test — provide a test seam instead.
Top-level declarations (functions, properties, `object`) obey the same posture — `public` is the language default and lands the declaration in the module ABI. A top-level function used only inside its file MUST be `private`; a top-level function reused across the module MUST be `internal`; `public` is reserved for surfaces named as external contracts. Prefer a `private` / `internal` top-level function over a stateless `object`-helper (per `AX_OBJECT_SINGLETON_STATELESS_ONLY`); prefer a top-level function over an extension when the receiver-relationship is weak (per `AX_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_DISCIPLINE`).

Kotlin idiomatic operators are mandatory: `?.`, `?:`, `?.let { }`, `takeIf { }`, `takeUnless { }`, destructuring (`val (a, b) = pair`), string templates (`"$x"`, `"${expr}"`). Avoid verbose `if`-checks for null / empty / bounds — the null-safety chain is the canonical replacement. Semantic density reduces visual noise and shrinks the surface for nullable-check bugs.

Scope functions have distinct contracts; the choice IS the intent. Enforced matrix:
| Function | Receiver ref inside | Returns | Use for | |---|---|---|---| | `let` | `it` | lambda result | null-safe transform (`x?.let { … }`); local rename for readability. | | `also` | `it` | receiver | side-effect on receiver (logging, adding to list) — receiver unchanged. | | `apply` | `this` | receiver | object initialization / builder — mutate the receiver, return it. | | `run` | `this` | lambda result | scoped compute on a receiver; conversion of receiver into another value. | | `with` | `this` | lambda result | focused block on a non-null receiver; not a chain call. |
Misuse (e.g. `apply` where `run`'s return semantics were needed; `also` where `let`'s transform was intended) is an anti-pattern per `AP_SCOPE_FUNCTION_MISUSE`. Nesting more than two scope functions is a refactor smell — extract a named function instead.

A name reflects a goal (teleology), not a pattern (topology). Forbidden semantic-noise names: `Manager`, `Handler`, `Data`, `Info`, `Wrapper`, `Helper`, `Util`, `do...`, `process...`. Pattern names tell the next agent nothing about business goal. `OrderFulfillmentPipeline` carries intent; `OrderManager` does not.

Use precise verbs. `retrieve` (not `get`), `verify` (not `check`), `compose` (not `make`), `resolve` (not `find`). Verbs encode the operation's contract. `get` is ambivalent; `retrieve` implies lookup in an external source with a possible failure path.
Kotlin note: this axiom governs FUNCTIONS that carry a get-shaped contract. Pure-getter surfaces belong in property syntax (`val name`) per `AX_PROPERTY_VS_FUNCTION`; the JVM-interop function form `getX()` is reserved for `@JvmStatic` bridges. Functions that fail the property criteria (I/O, throw, cost) MUST NOT be named `getX()` — pick the precise verb (`retrieveX`, `fetchX`, `resolveX`). No conflict with `AX_PROPERTY_VS_FUNCTION`: the choice is (property `val`) OR (function with a precise verb); `getX()`-as-function is out of scope outside JVM-interop.

Method name is a self-contained contract. Method names must be readable as a full contract outside the owner class (`verifyRegistrationData`, not just `validate` inside `UserValidator`). A reading agent often sees a method call without the owner class in focus (import, traceability grep). The name must carry meaning in isolation.

Public methods do not leak implementation. Forbidden infrastructure words in public APIs: `Db`, `Sql`, `Http`, `Retrofit`, `Room`, `Sqlite` (exception: serializer / adapter layers where the transport IS the contract). Leaking transport into a public name breaks Ports & Adapters and binds consumers to a concrete implementation.

Deliver exactly what the task and contract demand. No unrequested features, extension points, or optionality. Every extra API surface is a future refactor obligation and a source of drift from the contract.

Forbid premature abstractions. Do not extract an interface / sealed hierarchy / open class for logic that has ONE consumer and ONE concrete realization. Abstraction is justified only by confirmed variance or an explicit second consumer; otherwise it complicates grep and reading without payoff.

Minimal error surface. Handle only reachable errors. Do not defend against states proven impossible by types, `require` / `check` preconditions, or invariants. Kotlin's non-null defaults already close whole classes of NPEs — do not re-check what the type system enforces. Defense against the impossible is dead code — simulates reliability and obstructs reasoning about real failure paths.

Decompose by intent, not by volume. Avoid both monolithic functions AND artificial layering. Extract code only at TRUE intent boundaries that meaningfully improve readability, testability, or isolation. Splitting by line count without intent boundaries creates fictive functions that raise cognitive load without raising verifiability.

Every thrown exception message carries a Trace-Prefix. Format: `[ClassName#methodName]` or `[functionName]`. With cause-chains across several layers the only reliable way to recover the failure point is an explicit prefix; stack aggregators may truncate. Trace-Prefix is an error-message contract, NOT a logging directive — logging discipline is a separate project-level rule.

Preserve original context via the second parameter of Kotlin's `Exception(msg, cause)` constructors. Create and rethrow via `throw DomainException("[Trace-Prefix] ...", cause)`. NEVER transform `cause` — it is a lossless channel for the root cause; any transform breaks the debug chain. NEVER catch `CancellationException` and rethrow as a different type — cooperative cancellation depends on the identity of the exception (per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`).

Catch-Wrap-Rethrow is the only pattern in business-logic catch blocks. Wrap the caught exception with a domain exception carrying a Trace-Prefix and `cause`, then rethrow — nothing else. NEVER swallow, NEVER convert `Throwable` to a boolean / null / default value without an explicit `@invariant` naming the recovery contract. `CancellationException` is re-thrown as-is (do not wrap). Logging inside the catch is external policy — see the project-level logging rule.
Rationale: the Result-style discipline (returning a domain `Result` instead of throwing) is a scope-level architectural choice, not part of these baseline rules. When a scope adopts it, the scope's rule extends `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW` with an explicit Result mapping.

Validate arguments at the start of the function using Kotlin's stdlib preconditions: `require(cond) { "[Trace-Prefix] ..." }` for arguments, `requireNotNull(x) { "..." }` for nullable inputs, `check(cond) { "..." }` for internal state. Throw domain exceptions with context. Earlier validation = fewer state mutations before failure and clearer failure cause from the message.

Anchors: `//region START_[CONTEXT]_[INTENT]` / `//endregion END_[CONTEXT]_[INTENT]`. Uppercase tokens. Parity mandatory: every `START_X` must have `END_X` in the same file. The Kotlin IDE natively folds `//region`/`//endregion`; the uppercase `START_`/`END_` payload is an attention anchor for sliding-window LLMs and an XML-like span delimiter for long-context retrieval.
When a block has a non-obvious invariant or failure boundary, attach payload inside the anchor (outside it is detached from the block it protects): ONE payload kind → inline on the opening line `//region START_[NAME] — : `; 2+ kinds → separate `//` comment lines immediately after the opening anchor. Greppable: `//(region|endregion)\s+(START|END)_[A-Z0-9_]+`.

In a complex function wrap EVERY nested control-flow block with independent intent, side effects, or refactor risk: `if`/`else`, `for`, `while`, `when` (both statement and expression forms), `try`, `catch`, `finally`, and coroutine builders (`launch`, `async`, `withContext`). Do not skip anchors because the block looks short or locally readable. If another agent may need to isolate, patch, move, or audit the block as a unit, anchors are mandatory. This is patch-grammar, not cosmetic.

Do NOT wrap a trivial guard or single-action branch. Block has no independent policy, no meaningful side effect, no refactor hazard → anchors not needed. Single-expression `when` used purely as a value map, a lone Elvis fallback, a single-guard `require` — all skipped. An anchor around a single line is noise that dilutes the signal of mandatory anchors.
A `when` expression carrying a `throw` branch (per `AX_WHEN_EXHAUSTIVENESS`) is NOT a pure value map — the `else { throw ... }` is a failure boundary. Anchor is mandatory per `AX_ANCHOR_COVERAGE_NONTRIVIAL`; the trivial-exception carve-out does not apply.

Anchor name describes WHY the block exists. Does NOT restate syntax or literal conditions. `START_APPLY_FALLBACK_STRATEGY`, not `START_IF_NO_PATH`. `START_ENFORCE_RETRY_POLICY`, not `START_WHILE_ATTEMPTS_LT_MAX`. The name is the only way for a reader-agent to recognize the block's policy without reading the body.

All comments are agent-authored machine comments and MUST add intent that an agent cannot safely infer from syntax. A comment SUPPLEMENTS pretrained code understanding instead of fighting it: prefer the smallest local comment that increases recoverable intent / patch safety / invariant preservation. The next reader-agent has no access to the chat in which the code was written — a comment is the only context channel that does not derive from syntax. Excess comments compete with code and drift; insufficient comments force reconstruction from stack traces. Comments do NOT explain syntax to humans; in an AI-to-AI ecosystem, human narrative is noise.

Closed payload vocabulary: one or more of `purpose`, `consumer`, `invariant`, `side effect`, `failure mode`, `non-goal`. Use terse high-signal prose or `key: value` lines.
Forbidden: decorative prefixes (`// NOTE:`, `// IMPORTANT:`, `// TODO` without owner + ticket ref) — no machine semantics; narrating loops, branches, assignments, obvious names — steals credit from real policy comments; duplicating KDoc, types, signatures. NEVER write «temporary workaround» without (a) the cause, (b) the boundary of applicability, (c) what must remain unchanged — workaround without context is a mine for the next refactor.

Function body starts with executable code (typically a `require` / `check` guard). Hidden constraints belong in KDoc (`@invariant`, `@sideEffect`, `@throws`, `@pre`, `@post`); block-level invariants inside `//region START_` anchors. No narrative brief or rule-summary at method head — KDoc + signature is the canonical contract surface.

Comment iff removing it would hide a business rule, invariant, integration constraint, or refactor hazard. Pure data reshaping, obvious property getters, trivial guard clauses, straight-line pure computations are NOT commented — silence signals «no hidden policy here». A comment on trivial code falsely tells the agent to look for an invariant that does not exist; a missing comment on non-trivial code forces reverse-engineering.

`data class` is reserved for pure value-semantics: DTO, configuration snapshot, event payload, immutable projection. All properties `val`. `equals` / `hashCode` / `copy` are contractually generated — the value IS its content.
Regular `class` for entities with identity (a persistent order that survives field changes), for stateful services, and for anything whose equality is NOT structural. Never use `data class` for a domain entity — the auto-generated `equals` will silently redefine identity.
Equality contract for non-data `class`: - Default: keep identity equality (do NOT override `equals` / `hashCode`). A domain entity in a `Set` or `Map` key is compared by reference — this is usually the correct semantics for a mutable entity with a stable identifier field. - Override only when the domain contract demands business-key equality (e.g. `Order` equal iff `orderId` equal, regardless of instance). An override MUST come with a `@invariant` on the class KDoc naming the business key and the immutability requirement (business-key fields MUST be `val` — mutating them corrupts hash-based collections). - Mixing: NEVER partial (`equals` without `hashCode`, or vice versa). NEVER dependent on mutable `var` state.

`typealias` and `@JvmInline value class` cover different concerns — the choice is a type-safety decision, not a stylistic one.
- `typealias` is permitted ONLY to shorten complex generic signatures inside a bounded scope: function types (`typealias RequestHandler = suspend (Request) -> Response`), long parameterized types (`typealias PropertyEditor = suspend (T) -> Result`). Scope internal — never leaked as a public API rename of a plain type. - `typealias` on a domain primitive is FORBIDDEN (`typealias UserId = String` gives ZERO type safety — the compiler still accepts any `String` where `UserId` is expected, so parameter-swap bugs pass silently). Use `@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String)` instead — the compiler distinguishes it from `String` at every call site, and inlining erases the wrapper at runtime. - `@JvmInline value class` is the canonical channel for a domain identifier / bounded primitive: one `val` property, no additional state, no `init` block beyond validation, must be exported at the boundary where the primitive would otherwise leak. - Do NOT create a value class for a wrapper whose only purpose is future extensibility — YAGNI (`AX_NO_PREMATURE_ABSTRACTIONS`).

Declaration-site variance on generic types is a contract: the wrong choice becomes a compile-error obligation on every consumer that later needs the omitted direction. Enforced discipline:
- Producer types (a type that only PRODUCES `T` — return positions, output collections, sealed outcomes carrying `T`) → declare `out T`. Example: `sealed interface Result { data class Success(val value: T) : Result; data class Failure(val cause: Throwable) : Result }` — `out T` lets `Result` be assigned to `Result` cleanly. - Consumer types (a type that only CONSUMES `T` — parameter positions, sinks, comparators) → declare `in T`. - Invariant only when `T` appears in BOTH producer and consumer positions. - Use-site star-projection (`Result<*>`) permitted only inside implementation code where the type parameter is genuinely irrelevant; do NOT expose `Foo<*>` on a public API (loses type information at the boundary). - Rule of thumb (PECS — a Java-wildcard mnemonic; the Kotlin syntax is `out` / `in` as listed above, NOT `extends` / `super`): Producer → `out`, Consumer → `in`.

`enum class` for a closed set of discrete singleton values with no per-variant state (`OrderStatus.NEW | PAID | SHIPPED`). `sealed class` / `sealed interface` for a closed hierarchy where variants carry different shapes / state (`Result.Success(value) | Result.Failure(cause) | Result.Pending`). Never encode variant-specific state on an enum via nullable fields — that is a category error and defeats exhaustiveness.
`Nothing` as a type parameter and return type is a first-class contract, not a curiosity: - A variant of an `out T`-covariant sealed hierarchy that carries no `T` is declared `: Parent` (e.g. `data class Failure(val cause: Throwable) : Result`) — this keeps the variant assignment-compatible with any `Result` while preserving type safety at consumer positions. - A function that provably never returns (always throws) has return type `Nothing` — this lets the compiler treat any call site as terminating flow (crucial for `when`-expression exhaustiveness when the failure path is delegated to a helper). - `throw e` is itself an expression of type `Nothing`; that is precisely what makes `else { throw … }` in a `when`-expression satisfy exhaustiveness (per `AX_WHEN_EXHAUSTIVENESS`).

`when` used as an expression on a `sealed` or `enum` type is exhaustive by compiler enforcement — do NOT add an `else` branch that would silently absorb a new variant.
`when` used as a statement is NOT enforced by the compiler in the general case (a non-exhaustive statement form compiles with at most a warning under strict compiler flags — never a hard error by default). Therefore statement-form `when` on `sealed` / `enum` MUST be rewritten as an expression form (assign / return the result — even `Unit`) so exhaustiveness IS enforced: `val _: Unit = when (variant) { … }` or `return when (…) { … }`. Only when unhandled variants are a runtime invariant violation add `else { throw IllegalStateException("[Trace-Prefix] unexpected variant: $it") }` — never as a silent no-op. A silent `else {}` fallthrough on a sealed / enum is forbidden.

Kotlin classes are `final` by default — keep them so. Mark a class `open` only when polymorphism is confirmed (at least one concrete subclass or a documented extension point). `abstract` only for genuine templates. Avoid `open` on data classes — Kotlin already restricts it, and inheritance from data classes breaks `equals` invariants.

`companion object` is limited to: factory methods for the owning class, associated constants (`const val`), and `@JvmStatic` interop bridges. NEVER use companion as a pseudo-static state holder or a hidden singleton for logic — that erases DI seams and hides lifecycle from the reader.

Top-level `object` declarations are permitted for stateless helpers (pure functions grouped by domain), sealed hierarchy members (`object None : Result()`), and canonical instances of a marker type. A stateful service MUST NOT be declared as `object` — it defeats testability and DI. Statefulness includes any mutable field, cache, or reference to an I/O resource.

Domain prefix for types from external systems: `ApiOrder`, `VendorReservation`, `ErpCatalogItem`. Internal utilities have no prefix. The prefix protects a trust boundary: `Order` (internal) and `VendorOrder` (external) are different entities; conflating is a common source of domain bugs. Applies especially at serialization boundaries where a wire-format DTO must be distinguishable from a domain model.

Domain exceptions are declared via `class` (typically `open class DomainException(message: String, cause: Throwable? = null) : RuntimeException(message, cause)`) — never `typealias`. Only a real class participates in `is` / `catch` type-matching and preserves the type through the stack trace.

Mandatory protocol for direct implementations of a contract. For every exported runtime root that directly implements a named contract: 1. Keep the root-level `@purpose` (compressed essence). 2. Add `@implements {ContractName} in path` on the root class KDoc. 3. Add `@see {ContractName#memberName} in path` on every direct public/protected implementation member, unless that member is a true override with a full explicit contract.
Do not stop at the Kotlin `: ContractName` supertype declaration, class-level KDoc, or member «obviousness». These links are mandatory contract edges, not decoration. Without them a reader-agent does not see the implementation→contract link without grep; a member without `@see` is indistinguishable from an override.

File-level meta uses line-comments (`// @tag`), never a KDoc block — distinct syntactic class from entity KDoc so LLMs and grep distinguish file-scope from entity-scope unambiguously.
Block of consecutive `//` lines at the very top of the file, AFTER file-level annotations (`@file:JvmName(...)`, `@file:Suppress(...)`) and BEFORE the `package` declaration: `// @file: ` *(mandatory)* `// @consumers: ` *(optional; omit when no uniform consumer)* `// @tasks: [, TASK-ID...]` *(optional; may be added later)*
`@purpose` is NOT a file-level tag — it belongs exclusively to entities. Local entities inherit `@consumers` from file level and MUST NOT redeclare it unless their consumer diverges.
`@consumers:` and `@tasks:` are optional — a coding-only agent may lack full project context. Omit rather than fabricate.

Single-line KDoc for properties. When defining properties inside `data class`, `class`, or `interface`, generate the KDoc as a single flat string to preserve vertical density. If multiple tags are required, merge them on the same line using the ` | ` separator. Example: `/** @purpose Smallest id in the range | @invariant >= 0 */`. Multi-line KDoc blocks are strictly reserved for module roots, classes, and functions.
` | ` separates distinct KDoc **tags**, not continuation lines of one tag. A multi-sentence `@purpose` is compressed to one sentence — not joined with ` | `. Discard sentences that restate the property name or explain the obvious; keep only the constraint or role that cannot be inferred from the type.

Base KDoc contract shape for all classes, interfaces, objects, data classes, sealed hierarchies, functions, methods, properties, extension functions:
- **Default root contract:** `@purpose` (compressed essence). Do NOT replace a root definition or implementation owner with `@see`. - **Root implementation rule:** exported class or object directly implementing an existing named contract keeps its own `@purpose` AND adds `@implements {InterfaceName} in path`. - **Member implementation rule:** `@see {InterfaceName#memberName} in path` allowed only for direct public/protected implementation or override edge where behavior matches. - **Override rule:** override / redefinition (behavior/contract change) → write the full contract explicitly; do not rely only on `@see`. Kotlin `override` keyword requires the override to preserve or narrow the contract — encode the specialization in KDoc. - **Clarification rule:** if an implementation needs its own `@consumers`, `@invariant`, `@pre`, `@throws`, `@return`, `@post`, or `@sideEffect` because the inherited contract is being tightened/specialized/extended → treat as override; write the full explicit contract instead of mixing extra tags into a `@see`-only stub. - **Single-line:** `/** @purpose Verb Object Context */` or `/** @see {InterfaceName#memberName} in ./path */`. - **Multi-line:** for complex entities, exported implementation roots, or entities with optional tags. Strict order mandatory.
**Optional KDoc tags (order MANDATORY):** 1. `@consumers` — who consumes the API. 2. `@implements` — the contract root implemented. 3. `@invariant` — constraints, SLA, retry / error policies, ordering guarantees, implementation strategy guarantees that modifying agents must preserve. 4. `@pre` — hidden preconditions before the call. 5. `@param` — one coherent role description. Do NOT duplicate field structure from the type. 6. `@throws` — reason for throw (checked or unchecked; Kotlin has no `throws` clause — KDoc is the only channel). 7. `@return` — business purpose of a successful result / `suspend` resumption value. 8. `@post` — state guarantees after the call. 9. `@sideEffect` — I/O, network, DB, filesystem, coroutine dispatch, etc.
A strict order and closed vocabulary let a reader-agent parse the KDoc contract deterministically. File-level tags (`@file:`, `@consumers:`, `@tasks:`) live in `// @tag:` line-comments at file head — never inside entity KDoc (see `AX_FILE_LEVEL_CONTEXT`).

When each tag is used: - `@file:`, `@tasks:` — file-level line-comments only; see `AX_FILE_LEVEL_CONTEXT`. - `@consumers` — file-level line-comment when uniform; entity-level only when consumer diverges from file-level; skip for local helpers. - `@implements` — required on exported class/object root directly implementing a named interface/contract; skip for data shapes, interfaces, member declarations. - `@invariant` — stateful entities, resilience / error policy, ordering guarantees, non-local assumptions, coroutine cancellation semantics, dispatcher expectations. - `@pre` — ONLY for hidden environment / system-state preconditions not captured by the type signature or `require` / `check` guard. - `@param` — when arguments exist; one coherent role description; do NOT enumerate object fields already in the type. - `@throws` — when the function can throw (Kotlin does not encode this in the signature); describe failure reason, not generic possibility. For `suspend` functions, `CancellationException` is a special case — mention only if the function has non-trivial cancellation semantics (custom cleanup). - `@return` — for non-`Unit` results; describe WHY the caller needs the value, not the Kotlin shape. - `@post` — state guarantees not already encoded by `@return`, types, or obvious control flow. - `@sideEffect` — externally visible effects (network, fs, process, DB, shared-state mutation, emitted events, coroutine dispatch to a specific `Dispatcher`). Routine debug logging alone does NOT justify the tag. - `@see` — ONLY for direct member implementation / override of an existing contract; do NOT use as a root class/object tag when root owns runtime behavior. Behavior diverges → write the full contract.

Minimum requirements per entity kind: - **Data classes / exported data shapes:** `data class` + `@purpose`; use `@consumers` only when consumer diverges from the file-level context declaration; all properties `val`. - **Sealed hierarchies:** root-level `@purpose` describing the closed variant space; each variant has its own `@purpose` (unless a marker `object` with self-evident name). - **Pure alias / shape-forwarding exports** with no runtime behavior may use a root-level `@see`. But runtime-bearing class / object implementations do NOT replace their owner contract with `@see`. - **Service interfaces / external-system clients:** require `@invariant` for error policy, retry policy, ordering guarantees, rate limits, or other resilience constraints. Dispatcher documentation for `suspend` functions splits by ownership: - CALLER-required dispatcher (function does NOT switch context internally; caller must run it on a specific dispatcher) → `@invariant Dispatcher: MUST be called on `. - INTERNALLY-managed dispatcher (function uses `withContext(...)` in its own body) → `@sideEffect Dispatch: `; do NOT add a `@invariant Dispatcher:` — that would falsely obligate the caller. - Dispatcher-agnostic (pure suspend, no `withContext` and no dispatcher requirement) → no dispatcher tag needed. - **Implementations of an existing runtime contract:** owner-level `@purpose` on class/object + `@implements {ContractName} in path` on root + `@see {ContractName#memberName} in path` on each public/protected member when behavior matches. - **`suspend` functions:** `@return` describes the resumption value; `@throws` describes both regular exceptions and non-trivial cancellation cleanup; `@sideEffect` documents external action AND dispatch destination when relevant. - **Exported config constants:** `@invariant` when value bounds or combinations must remain stable. - **Extension functions:** the receiver type MUST be a domain type where the extension genuinely belongs; a generic-receiver extension (`fun Any?.…`) is forbidden unless it is a stdlib-style null-safety operator on a value class. - **Within one implementing surface** `@implements` and member-level `@see` MUST use the same path style and same contract names — do not mix local-relative and project-root-relative references inside one module.

Exception handling is mandatory in business logic. Any business function with network/file/process I/O, DB access, mutation of external state, or integration with an external system MUST wrap the failure point in `try`/`catch` per `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`. Missing try/catch on an integration boundary turns any transient failure into an un-traced un-contextualized exception. `CancellationException` MUST be re-thrown as-is inside the catch and MUST NOT be wrapped.
Flow producer bodies: the «mandatory wrap around the I/O call» is satisfied by ONE of the two channels below — never required in both places at once. Pick per intent: - Producer-local recovery (fallback value, per-call retry, mapping to a domain outcome variant) → `try`/`catch` inside the builder per `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`. - Downstream recovery (retry-with-backoff for the whole flow, fallback flow, terminal error handling) → the `catch { }` operator at the collector side, which explicitly does NOT catch `CancellationException`. Naked propagation (no `try/catch`, no `catch { }` operator) is forbidden — an unhandled I/O exception in a producer surfaces at collect time without Trace-Prefix / cause preservation.

Structured concurrency is mandatory. Enforced rules: - `GlobalScope` is forbidden — every coroutine belongs to a lexically-scoped `CoroutineScope` owned by a lifecycle (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope, an explicitly held scope with `SupervisorJob` + owned dispatcher). - `runBlocking` is forbidden outside three permitted contexts: the JVM `main` entry point, tests, and CLI `main` scripts. Bridging between suspend and non-suspend code inside business logic uses `withContext` on the appropriate dispatcher, not `runBlocking`. - Dispatchers are explicit at every I/O and CPU-bound boundary: `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` for blocking I/O, `withContext(Dispatchers.Default)` for CPU-bound work. UI code enters the UI dispatcher only when writing to the UI surface. - Concurrent-independent branches (fan-out where one failure must not cancel siblings) use `supervisorScope` / `SupervisorJob`; concurrent-dependent branches (all-or-nothing) use `coroutineScope`. - CPU-bound long-running loops without any `suspend` call in the body invoke `ensureActive()` at each iteration to cooperate with cancellation. Loops that already contain a `suspend` call per iteration (network, DB, `delay`, `yield`) do NOT need `ensureActive()` — the suspension point IS the cooperation point; adding `ensureActive()` there is dead code and a false «no suspension here» signal per `AX_MINIMAL_ERROR_SURFACE`. - `CancellationException` MUST propagate — never caught and swallowed. A `catch (e: Throwable)` that intends to handle only I/O errors MUST explicitly rethrow `CancellationException` first, or catch a narrower type. - `async` results (`Deferred`) MUST be `.await()`-ed within the same scope — an orphaned `Deferred` is a resource leak. - **`Flow` producers exception.** Two distinct constraints apply, per builder kind: - `flow { }` (cold `FlowCollector` builder): `emit(x)` inside a `withContext(...)` block throws `IllegalStateException` (Flow's context-preservation invariant). Cold producers place the dispatcher via `.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` on the flow itself instead — see `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`. - `callbackFlow { }` / `channelFlow { }` (`ProducerScope` builders): there is NO `emit` method at all — the API is `channel.send` / `channel.trySend`. `withContext` around `send` / `trySend` is fine. Do not confuse the two APIs; the compiler already prevents `emit` here at the type level. - Operator bodies (`map` / `transform`): `withContext` is unrestricted — the operator's own return value / receiver's `emit` outside the `withContext` block carries the element; no context-preservation violation.

`Flow` / `SharedFlow` / `StateFlow` are the canonical async-stream API and carry contracts that plain `suspend` functions do not. Enforced discipline:
- **Dispatcher placement.** Producer-side dispatcher is set on the flow with `.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` at the earliest point where the upstream work becomes blocking. NEVER wrap `flowOn` around the `collect` call — `flowOn` affects upstream, not downstream. Collection itself runs on the collector's context (lifecycleScope / viewModelScope in Android UI). - **Collection scope.** Every `collect` / `collectLatest` MUST run inside a lifecycle-owned `CoroutineScope` (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, an owned scope with `SupervisorJob`). NEVER collect from `GlobalScope`; NEVER collect inside a suspend function whose scope is unclear — pass the scope explicitly or accept the `Flow` and let the caller collect. - **`callbackFlow` cleanup.** A `callbackFlow { }` builder MUST end with `awaitClose { … }` that unregisters the callback / listener / subscription. Omitting `awaitClose` leaks the subscription past cancellation; the compiler will not warn. - **Buffering bounds.** `SharedFlow(replay = N, extraBufferCapacity = M)` / `MutableStateFlow` with any non-default buffer requires an `@invariant` on the declaring property naming the upper bound and its rationale. An unbounded buffer (`BufferOverflow.SUSPEND` on an infinite hot producer) is forbidden without a documented back-pressure strategy — silent unbounded growth is a design-evident leak. - **Hot vs cold intent.** `flow { }` is cold — every collector re-runs the producer; `StateFlow` / `SharedFlow` are hot — shared state / multicast. Convert cold→hot via `stateIn` / `shareIn` only with an explicit scope + `SharingStarted` policy; the policy IS the contract (WhileSubscribed / Eagerly / Lazily) and MUST match the consumer lifecycle. - **Terminal operators inside flow.** NEVER call `collect` / `toList` on another `Flow` inside a `flow { }` builder — this is a downstream operation smuggled into upstream and defeats laziness. To nest / merge another `Flow` into a producer, use `flatMapConcat` / `flatMapMerge` / `flatMapLatest` at the call site. `map` / `transform` are for element-by-element transformation, not for nesting a `collect`. - **Error boundaries in producers.** I/O inside a `flow { }` / `callbackFlow { }` / `channelFlow { }` body that can fail MUST be wrapped per `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`. `CancellationException` is re-thrown as-is — a producer that catches `CancellationException` and swallows it breaks cooperative Flow cancellation. For downstream error handling (retry, fallback), prefer the operator `catch { }` (which explicitly does NOT catch `CancellationException`) at the collector side; use a `try / catch` inside the producer only when the recovery is producer-local. - **`stateIn` / `shareIn` scope.** The `scope` passed to `stateIn` / `shareIn` MUST be a lifecycle-owned scope (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, an explicit owned scope with `SupervisorJob`) — never `GlobalScope`, per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`. `GlobalScope` on `stateIn` / `shareIn` creates a hot Flow that outlives every consumer and accumulates subscribers — design-evident leak.

Extension functions must express a natural receiver relationship: the extension reads as «this thing knows how to». Do NOT create extensions to hide a utility as a method. Forbidden patterns: - Extension on `Any?` / `Any` for domain logic (loses type safety). - Extension whose body doesn't reference the receiver. - Extension on a widely-shared stdlib type that changes its behavior for one module — pollutes IDE completion globally.
When the receiver relationship is weak, write a plain top-level function with the receiver as the first parameter.

Choose property (`val name: T`) vs function (`fun getName(): T`) by contract: - Property = pure, cheap, side-effect-free, deterministic; may compute but must not throw for typical inputs; must not perform I/O; must not have observable timing cost. - Function = anything that fails any property criterion: I/O, non-trivial cost, potential exception, side effect, non-determinism.
Kotlin syntax collapses property access and getter call — the reader assumes property semantics. Violating the property contract (`val user: User` that hits the DB) breaks the reader's mental model.

Definitions.Definition: Trace-Prefix format: `[ClassName#methodName]` or `[functionName]`. Used in all thrown Error / Exception messages.

Complex (triggers non-trivial anchors + full KDoc optional-tag set) if any: network/file/process/DB I/O; shared-state mutation; retry/fallback/error translation; concurrency, `launch`/`async`/`withContext`, structured cancellation, locking, batching. OR any two of: multiple decision points, hidden pre/postconditions, nested control flow, non-local refactor hazard.

Closed vocabulary for machine comments: `purpose`, `consumer`, `invariant`, `side effect`, `failure mode`, `non-goal`. Inside tests, additionally allowed: `contract` and `observation focus` (per project testing directive).

Pattern.Intent: Exported data shape as `data class` (all `val`); file-level line-comment header; single-line KDoc per property; no duplication of Kotlin structure.
Pattern.Why: Data shape with no runtime behavior → `data class` + entity `@purpose`. Shared context declared once in file-level `// @file:` / `// @consumers:` header; entity does NOT redeclare `@consumers`. All properties `val` per `AX_IMMUTABILITY_DEFAULT`.

Pattern.Intent: Closed variant space via `sealed`; exhaustive `when` on the sealed type without `else`.
Pattern.Why: `sealed interface` closes the variant space; `when` used as expression is exhaustive by compiler — no `else` (per `AX_WHEN_EXHAUSTIVENESS`). Adding a fourth variant is a compile error at every `when` — the invariant is enforced by the language.

Pattern.Intent: Service interface: precise optional-tag order, SLA in `@invariant`, side effects and dispatcher expectations exposed explicitly.
Pattern.Why: `interface` because this is a polymorphism point (Port), not a data shape. Invariants encode resilience policy (retry, error wrapping) that consumers must respect. Dispatcher documentation follows the INTERNALLY-managed case of `AX_ENTITY_SPECIFIC_MINIMUMS`: implementations own the `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` switch, so the tag is `@sideEffect Dispatch:` — an `@invariant Dispatcher: MUST be called on …` would falsely obligate the caller.

Pattern.Intent: Implementation of an existing contract: root keeps `@purpose` + `@implements`; inherited members use `@see`; function body starts with `require` guard; non-trivial blocks wrapped in compact-form `//region START_...` / `//endregion END_...` anchors; Catch-Wrap-Rethrow.
Pattern.Why: All mandatory protocols together: `// @file:` header, `@implements` on root, `@see` on member, executable-first body (`require` guard), compact single-payload anchor (invariant inlined on `//region` line), Trace-Prefixed exception, cause-chain, explicit `Dispatchers.IO`, `CancellationException` re-thrown as-is per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`.

Pattern.Intent: Concurrent-independent fan-out: `supervisorScope` so one failure does not cancel siblings; explicit dispatcher; each `async` is awaited within the same scope.
Pattern.Why: Independent failures require `supervisorScope`; a plain `coroutineScope` would cancel all siblings on the first failure per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`. Every `async` is `.await()`-ed within the same scope — no orphan `Deferred`. Dispatcher is explicit at the I/O boundary.

Pattern.Intent: Scope functions selected by intent per matrix; not swapped for aesthetic reasons.
Pattern.Why: `?.let` is the canonical null-safe transform (per `AX_SCOPE_FUNCTION_CHOICE`); Elvis fallback expresses the absent-value contract from the property KDoc. Anchors omitted per `AX_ANCHOR_TRIVIAL_EXCEPTION` — single-expression body, no independent policy inside.

AntiPattern.Bad: `val name = user!!.profile!!.name` inside a function body with no `@invariant` on the enclosing block or method KDoc.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: `!!` names no runtime guarantee (violates `AX_NULL_SAFETY_STRICT`); reader-agent cannot recover why the assertion is safe. Chained `!!` is exponential landmine surface.

AntiPattern.Bad: `var currentState: OrderState = OrderState.NEW` at class body with no `@invariant` explaining mutation lifecycle; property is exposed public.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Public `var` on a domain state without an invariant means any consumer can mutate it at any time. Violates `AX_IMMUTABILITY_DEFAULT` and `AX_TRUTHFUL_VISIBILITY`.
AntiPattern.Good: ```kotlin /** * @purpose Current lifecycle state of the order. * @invariant Transitions driven exclusively by OrderLifecycle#transition; external mutation forbidden. */ private var _currentState: OrderState = OrderState.NEW val currentState: OrderState get() = _currentState ```

AntiPattern.Bad: `enum class Result { SUCCESS, FAILURE; var value: String? = null; var cause: Throwable? = null }` with per-instance mutation of `value` / `cause`.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Encoding variant-specific state on an enum via nullable fields defeats exhaustiveness and creates «which fields are valid on which variant» invariant that lives outside the type. Category error per `AX_SEALED_VS_ENUM`.

AntiPattern.Bad:
`fun start() { GlobalScope.launch { doWork() } }` inside a service; or `fun query(): List
= runBlocking { db.fetchAll() }` inside business logic.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: `GlobalScope` has no lifecycle — leaks coroutines past the owning service; `runBlocking` in business logic blocks the calling thread and defeats structured concurrency. Violates `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`.

AntiPattern.Bad: `user.apply { logger.info("touched $name") }` — using `apply` where the intent is a side-effect log (returns receiver ignored); `builder.also { it.build() }` — using `also` where the intent is transform (`.build()` result is discarded).
AntiPattern.WhyBad: `apply` and `also` return the receiver — a discarded receiver is dead code. Violates `AX_SCOPE_FUNCTION_CHOICE`. The intent of the code disagrees with the semantics the reader-agent is trained to expect.

AntiPattern.Bad: `try { … } catch (e: Exception) { throw ServiceError("failed") }` — Trace-Prefix missing, `cause` dropped, `CancellationException` accidentally swallowed.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Cause dropped → debug chain lost (`AX_ERROR_CHAINING_CAUSE`); no Trace-Prefix (`AX_TRACE_PREFIXED_ERRORS`); `catch (e: Exception)` will catch `CancellationException` and re-throw a different type — breaks cooperative cancellation (`AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`).

AntiPattern.Bad:
`fun items(): MutableList
= _items` — exposing internal mutable collection through public API.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Consumers can silently mutate internal state; the ownership boundary is broken. Violates `AX_IMMUTABILITY_DEFAULT`.
AntiPattern.Good:
```kotlin fun items(): List
= _items.toList() // OR when the API needs live-view semantics: val items: List
get() = _items ```

AntiPattern.Bad: `open class OrderRepository(private val db: Db) { open fun findById(id: OrderId): Order? = … }` with no confirmed subclass or documented extension point — `open` added «in case someone wants to extend».
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Speculative `open` is a hidden contract obligation (Liskov, override safety) with no consumer. Violates `AX_OPEN_BY_INTENT` and `AX_NO_PREMATURE_ABSTRACTIONS`.

AntiPattern.Bad: Anchors around a single `val` or a single-return `when`; anchor name `START_CHECK_RETRIES` (names syntax, not intent); comment restates the `if`; `IllegalStateException("Limit")` without Trace-Prefix or cause.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Atomic noise (violates `AX_ANCHOR_TRIVIAL_EXCEPTION`); name violates `AX_ANCHOR_INTENTFUL_NAMES`; comment violates `AX_COMMENT_VOCABULARY`; exception violates `AX_TRACE_PREFIXED_ERRORS`, `AX_ERROR_CHAINING_CAUSE`.

Hook.Purpose: Kotlin code compiles cleanly (no unresolved refs, no type errors, no `!!` propagating through nullable inference).
Hook.Expected: Exit 0; empty stderr warnings for changed files.

Hook.Purpose: Android Lint on debug variant — catches lifecycle, Context-leak, and API-level issues.
Smoke-grep for forbidden constructs on changed files.
Hook.Expected: Empty (no matches) on new/changed non-entry non-test files. Matches allowed only in `Main.kt`, standard test source-sets (`test`, `androidTest`, `commonTest`, `jvmTest`, `sharedTest`), test fixtures / utilities, and blocks carrying an explicit `@invariant`-anchored justification.

Hook.Purpose: Smoke-grep for terminal operators (`.collect`, `.toList`) called on another `Flow` inside a `flow { }` builder — the smuggling anti-pattern forbidden by `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`.
Hook.Expected: Advisory smoke only, NOT a hard gate. The regex does not track brace nesting: it flags any `.collect` / `.toList` within 400 chars after a `flow {` opening, whether inside or after the builder body. Manually inspect each match — the finding is a violation ONLY when `.collect` / `.toList` is inside the producer block on another `Flow`; rewrite that case via `flatMapConcat` / `flatMapMerge` / `flatMapLatest` per `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`. Long producer bodies (>400 chars) escape detection — do not treat empty output as proof of compliance.

Hook.Purpose: Verify anchor parity and enable agent grep-navigation: every `//region START_X` must have `//endregion END_X` in the same file.
Hook.Expected: For every `START_NAME` occurrence there is a matching `END_NAME` in the same file; counts equal per file.

KotlinCodingRules.RewardCriteria:
✅ File has `// @file:` line-comment header (after `@file:` annotations, before `package`); `// @consumers:` / `// @tasks:` when applicable; no `@purpose` at file level. ✅ Every exported entity has valid KDoc contract per `AX_BASE_CONTRACT_SHAPE`; tag order preserved. ✅ Implementation roots use `@purpose` + `@implements`; member implementations use `@see`; overrides write the full contract. ✅ Comments carry intent (purpose / consumer / invariant / side effect / failure mode / non-goal); do NOT restate syntax. ✅ Anchors on every non-trivial control-flow block; intent-named, not syntax-named; paired `START_X`/`END_X`; compact single-line form when one payload kind, multi-line when 2+. ✅ Trivial guards, single-expression `when`, single-action branches NOT wrapped in anchors. ✅ Exception messages contain Trace-Prefix; rethrow preserves `cause`; catch blocks follow Catch-Wrap-Rethrow; `CancellationException` re-thrown as-is. ✅ Modern Kotlin operators (`?.`, `?:`, `?.let`, `takeIf`, destructuring, string templates) instead of verbose null-checks. ✅ `val` default; `var` justified by `@invariant`; public collections `List` / `Set` / `Map` (not mutable). ✅ Visibility precise: `private` for local state, `internal` for module contracts, `public` only for external surfaces, `protected` only for open inheritance edges; language default omitted. ✅ Scope functions chosen by intent per matrix; no misuse of `apply`/`also` return semantics. ✅ `data class` for value-semantics DTO; regular `class` for entities with identity; `sealed` for closed hierarchies with per-variant state; `enum` for discrete stateless values. ✅ `when` on `sealed` / `enum` exhaustive without `else`; `else` present only as invariant-violation throw. ✅ Classes `final` by default; `open` only with confirmed polymorphism. ✅ `companion object` used for factory / constants only; `object` singletons stateless only. ✅ Coroutines structured: no `GlobalScope`; `runBlocking` only in permitted entry contexts; dispatchers explicit at I/O / CPU boundary; `supervisorScope` for concurrent-independent, `coroutineScope` for concurrent-dependent; `ensureActive()` in long loops; every `async` awaited within the same scope. ✅ Names express teleology (business goal), not topology (pattern); precise verbs; public names do NOT leak transport. ✅ External-system types carry domain prefix; domain exceptions declared via `class`. ✅ Extension functions have a natural receiver relationship; not utility-in-disguise. ✅ Property vs function chosen by contract (property = pure/cheap/no-throw/no-I/O).
❌ Bare `!!` outside an `@invariant`-anchored block that names the guarantee. ❌ `var` on public API without an `@invariant` explaining mutation lifecycle. ❌ `MutableList` / `MutableSet` / `MutableMap` on public API surface. ❌ `GlobalScope` in production code; `runBlocking` in business logic; missing dispatcher at I/O boundary; orphaned `Deferred`. ❌ `catch (e: Exception)` / `catch (e: Throwable)` that does not re-throw `CancellationException`. ❌ Exception without Trace-Prefix or without `cause` on rethrow inside business logic. ❌ Missing try/catch on integration boundary of a business function. ❌ Comments that restate loops/branches/assignments, or duplicate KDoc. ❌ Anchors around atomic operations (lone return, single val) or with syntax-style names. ❌ Missing anchor on non-trivial block with independent policy / side effect / refactor hazard. ❌ Scope function misuse: `apply` where return semantics ignored; `also` used as transform. ❌ `data class` used for entities with identity; `enum` with nullable variant-specific state. ❌ `when` on `sealed` / `enum` with a silent `else` no-op that would absorb a new variant. ❌ Speculative `open` without confirmed polymorphism; premature interface for a single consumer. ❌ Extension function on `Any?` / `Any` for domain logic; extension whose body ignores the receiver. ❌ Property performing I/O, throwing for typical inputs, or with observable timing cost (should be a function). ❌ Mismatched KDoc tag order; duplication of Kotlin type fields in `@param`/`@return`; `@see` on a runtime-bearing root instead of `@purpose` + `@implements`. ❌ Mixed implementation reference style (local-relative and project-root-relative `@implements`/`@see` in one module).
